faq.q: Is fibrocystic disease a precursor to breast cancer?

faq.a: Yes, breastfeeding is safe and may even reduce future cyst formation.
faq.q: Can I breastfeed with fibrocystic breasts?

faq.a: Caffeine can increase estrogen activity and cause fluid retention, worsening cystic pain in susceptible women.

exam: What history points help differentiate fibrocystic change from carcinoma? — Cyclical pain, bilateral lumpiness, fluctuant cysts, no skin changes.
A 28‑year‑old woman presents with a tender 2 cm breast lump that fluctuates with her cycle. What is your next step? — Perform focused breast ultrasound; if cystic, consider aspiration.
How would you manage a large, painful cyst when ultrasound is unavailable? — Perform blind fine‑needle aspiration; if clear fluid obtained and pain improves, reassure and follow up.
Which medication would you avoid for chronic breast pain in a smoker over 35 years and why? — Combined oral contraceptive; increased risk of venous thromboembolism.
What red‑flag feature would prompt immediate referral for imaging? — Persistent unilateral hard mass >2 cm with skin changes.

Explain why fibroadenoma is often mistaken for fibrocystic disease and how to distinguish them. — Both are mobile; fibroadenoma is solid, painless, and does not vary with menstrual cycle; ultrasound shows solid hypoechoic mass.

In a low‑resource clinic, a patient cannot afford ultrasound. How do you safely rule out malignancy? — Detailed history, thorough physical exam, assess red‑flags, and arrange referral if any concerning feature persists.
What lifestyle advice reduces symptoms of fibrocystic change? — Limit caffeine and high‑fat foods, wear supportive bras, and maintain regular exercise.
ai.title: Fibrocystic Breast Disease
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Fibrocystic change is a benign, hormone‑related disorder causing lumpy, painful breasts. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by focused imaging when available. Management focuses on reassurance, lifestyle modification and symptom control.

b: Diagnosis is clinical: diffuse or focal breast lumpiness, tenderness, often worsening pre‑menstrually.
Confirmatory imaging (ultrasound or mammography) shows multiple cysts or heterogeneous echo texture; not required if classic presentation.
sections.p: A common benign breast condition characterised by fibrosis, cyst formation and stromal edema, leading to palpable nodularity and cyclic pain.

b: Mild: occasional discomfort, cysts <1 cm, no functional limitation.
Moderate: regular pain, cysts 1–3 cm, may affect daily activities.
Severe: constant pain, cysts >3 cm, anxiety about cancer, may need procedural intervention.
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden and cyst size rather than a formal stage system.

b: Estrogen‑dominant state (luteal phase, oral contraceptives, pregnancy).
High dietary caffeine or fat intake.
Local infection or inflammation (e.g., mastitis, TB breast).
HIV‑related immune dysregulation may exaggerate breast changes.
Herbal remedies containing phytoestrogens.
sections.p: Hormonal fluctuations are the primary driver, with additional contributors common in low‑resource settings.

b: Tenderness that peaks 2–3 days before menses and resolves with menstruation.
Palpable mobile cysts, sometimes fluctuant.
No skin changes, nipple discharge is rare and non‑bloody.
sections.p: Patients report cyclic breast pain, heaviness, and a “lumpy” feel, often bilateral but can be unilateral.
Targeted tests answer specific clinical questions; when imaging is unavailable, rely on history and physical exam.

t.b: Is the lump cystic or solid? Cystic lesions appear anechoic with posterior enhancement; solid lesions need further evaluation.

t.a: Fine‑needle aspiration (FNA) of a dominant cyst
t.b: Does the cyst contain clear fluid? Clear fluid with symptom relief confirms benign cyst; bloody or purulent fluid prompts cytology.
Are there suspicious calcifications or masses? Absence of suspicious features supports benign diagnosis.
Is the patient pregnant? Pregnancy influences management and hormone‑related pain.

b: Persistent unilateral mass >2 cm not fluctuating with cycle.
Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or bloody discharge.
Rapid growth, weight loss, fever – consider breast abscess or TB.
sections.p: Identify features that suggest malignancy or infection.

b: Lifestyle: reduce caffeine, wear supportive bra, limit high‑fat diet.
Analgesia: NSAIDs (ibuprofen) for pain; avoid aspirin in patients with bleeding risk.
Large symptomatic cysts: ultrasound‑guided aspiration; repeat if recurs.
Refractory pain: consider low‑dose oral contraceptive to stabilise hormone swings; avoid in smokers >35 y or thrombotic risk.
Educate: reassure benign nature, teach self‑examination.
sections.p: Treat symptoms, modify risk factors, and intervene on large cysts when needed.

b: Re‑evaluate at 6 months; earlier if new concerning signs appear.
Encourage monthly self‑exam; refer for imaging if any new hard or fixed area.
Address modifiable factors annually (caffeine, diet, bra fit).
sections.p: Regular review ensures symptom control and early detection of any change.

b: Breast carcinoma – usually hard, fixed, painless, may have skin changes.
Breast abscess – painful, erythematous, often febrile, purulent discharge.
Fibroadenoma – well‑circumscribed, mobile, painless, common in younger women.
Ultrasound may miss microcalcifications suggestive of cancer.
Negative FNA does not exclude underlying carcinoma; persistent mass warrants repeat imaging.
Hormone assays are not routinely useful and can distract from clinical assessment.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in size of a unilateral mass
Skin ulceration, nipple retraction, or bloody discharge
Fever with breast pain suggesting abscess
